ticket.title: Plugin skills marked disable-model-invocation can't be used when a person asks in words (handoff, record-session, tickets, update-plan)
ticket.body:
## What happened

On 2026-10-14 the owner asked a Claude Code session, in plain words, to "send a handoff to get that stuff in". The session tried to load the `trov:handoff` skill, and Claude Code refused:

> Skill trov:handoff cannot be used with Skill tool due to disable-model-invocation. Ask the user to run /trov:handoff themselves — it cannot be invoked via the Skill tool. Do not replicate this skill's workflow by other means

So the session told the owner it couldn't send handoffs, and gave them a prompt to paste into another chat instead. The owner had to push back ("you can send handoffs, what do you mean") before the session called `send_handoff` over MCP directly (handoff #7). That worked first time, but without the skill's guidance on the context shape, the 300-word body or the session id.

## Why

`plugins/trov/skills/handoff/SKILL.md` sets `disable-model-invocation: true`. The intent, per its description, is "explicit invocation only — must never auto-fire at a natural stopping point". But the flag blocks every case where the model loads the skill, including a person asking for it **in words**. Only a typed `/trov:handoff` gets through. The harness then tells the model not to do the work by other means, so the most likely outcome is a refusal, even though the MCP tool is right there.

The same flag is on `record-session`, `tickets` and `update-plan`, so "record this session", "file a ticket for that" and "update the plan" hit the same wall.

ticket.title: Repo dashboard: log ingestion (errors and log volume per environment)
ticket.body:
Ingest application logs so the Repo dashboard can show errors and log volume next to deploys and health, not only request counts and error rates.

## Scope

Pull logs, or a summary of them, from where each environment already runs: Cloudflare Workers (Logpush or Workers Logs / Observability), Railway, and, once #97 lands, the hosting providers (Vercel, Render, Netlify, Fly.io). The org admin enters the credential in Org settings › Integrations, the same way Cloudflare analytics and Railway are set up today.

Store aggregates and the top recurring errors, not raw log lines: error counts per environment per hour, the most frequent messages (grouped and scrubbed), and the first time each was seen.

## Done when

- An admin can connect a log source for an environment, and Test connection passes against the real API.
- The Repo dashboard shows that environment's error volume and its top recurring errors, and links each one to the deploy it started after.
- Nothing on a render path calls the provider: reads come from D1, and capture happens in the cron or Poll now.
- Credentials go only to the provider's own API host, log text is scrubbed before it is stored, and an org with no log source costs no requests.
- Retention is bounded, the same way `hx_*` metrics are pruned.

Depends on #97 for the non-Cloudflare and non-Railway hosts.

ticket.title: Let a person delete their own account from Settings
ticket.body:
## Problem

There is no way to delete an account in the app. The Terms and the Privacy Policy both say to write to hello@trov.dev, so today it is a manual job for the operator, and a person who wants out has no button.

## Wanted

A "Delete account" action in the personal Settings screen (the Session tile, away from Sign out), behind a confirmation that names what will happen and asks the person to type their handle.

## What deleting has to deal with

1. **Organizations the person OWNS.**
   - With other members: ownership must go to someone else first, or the delete is refused with a list of those organizations and a link to each one's Members tab.
   - With nobody else in it: the organization goes too. Say so, by name, in the confirmation.
   - With a live subscription: refused until it is cancelled. The Terms already say deleting an account does not cancel a subscription; here it must be impossible to leave one running with no owner.
2. **Organizations the person is only a member of.** They are removed, which frees a seat, exactly as an admin removing them does.
3. **What they wrote.** The Privacy Policy says content written in a team's workspace may stay with that team, attributed to the handle. Decide between keeping the handle on that content, or replacing it with a neutral "deleted account" marker. The second is the stronger privacy answer and needs every handle column (`HANDLE_COLUMNS`) rewritten, the way a rename does.

ticket.title: One GitHub account, several Trov organizations: connect different repositories to different orgs
ticket.body:
## Problem

People want different Trov organizations for different repositories — a personal org for one project, a client's org for another — while all of those repositories live under ONE GitHub account. Today that cannot be set up through the GitHub App.

`docs/architecture/github-app.md` states the rule: **"An installation belongs to at most one org, and an org has at most one live installation."** An installation is one GitHub account (a user or a GitHub organization). So once the Trov App on `AndresL230` is bound to one Trov organization, no second Trov organization can use it, whatever repositories that account holds. The second org is left with the manual path: a pasted token and a hand-made webhook.

A related limit sits beside it: **an organization captures only its primary repository.** The plan table already sells more (Free 1, Pro 5 repositories), and a second repository can be listed, but its pull requests, CI and deploys are not captured.

## Wanted

1. **One installation, many organizations — split by repository.** The same GitHub account's App installation can be used by more than one Trov organization, each bound to the specific repositories it was given. Repository A is tracked by org X, repository B by org Y.
2. **Still exactly one organization per repository.** A repository's events land in one organization, never two. That guarantee is what keeps one team's pull requests out of another's dashboard; it moves from "one org per installation" to "one org per repository".

ticket.title: Instant intelligence · use: a reading list when someone claims a handoff
ticket.body:
Part of #154. Depends on the building blocks.

When a handoff is claimed, show a short 'read these first' list: the docs and decisions that bear on the task.

**Why:** it shortens the first ten minutes of a session.

**Careful:** this is mostly retrieval over what Trov already indexes, ranked; say so, and never present it as complete.

## Rules that bind every one of these (CLAUDE.md)

- **Suggestions, never actions.** A model may propose a label, an order or a destination. It never closes, reassigns, promotes, publishes or deletes anything: nothing infers a resolution, and agents stage while humans confirm.
- **Never while a page loads.** A judgement is made when something is written, or in a scheduled run, and stored. Nothing on a render path calls a model.
- **A fixed set of answers.** The model picks from a list Trov gives it; it does not write interface, markup or figures.
- **Never guess on read.** No suggestion is shown as fact; an item with no suggestion simply has none.
- **Metered.** Calls count against a per-organization allowance in `PLANS`.

ticket.title: Explore: instant intelligence — fast, cheap judgements attached to what Trov already stores
ticket.body:
## The idea

A fast, inexpensive model looks at something Trov already holds — a feed entry, a ticket, a proposal, an item in Unplaced — and attaches a small structured judgement to it: a priority, a category, a tag, a destination, a risk. The interface stays hand-built and simply sorts, groups, filters or suggests by that judgement.

The model classifies and ranks. It does not generate the screen. That is what makes it cheap, and what makes it safe to use in many places.

## Why it could matter

Trov's bottleneck is human attention: what to review first, where an unplaced item belongs, which of forty feed entries matters to me. Every one of those is a small judgement over text Trov already has.

## Shape of the work

**Building blocks first** (so this is one capability used in many places, not ten separate features), then the uses, most valuable first. Each is its own issue, listed in a comment below.

ticket.title: Guided repository setup: pick the stack, then be walked through connecting each piece and where to get its keys
ticket.body:
## Decision (owner, 2026-10-10)

Trov does not work out how a repository is hosted by reading it. **It asks.** When someone sets up a repository in an organization they get a short guided setup: they say what the stack is, and Trov then connects each piece with them, telling them exactly where to get each key as they go. At the end the Repo dashboard is the one that fits what they said.

This settles the open question in #147 for the first version: no file is opened, and no model is needed to know the stack. Detection from events Trov already captures (the hosting branch's "Detected: Vercel") only PRE-FILLS an answer; the person confirms it.

## The flow

1. **Repository.** Pick it (the GitHub App's repository picker; the manual path stays for those who cannot install the App).
2. **What is it?** One question with plain choices, each with a one-line description and a small picture of the dashboard it leads to:
   - One service that does everything (a Worker, a single app server)
   - A frontend and a backend, hosted separately
   - A static site
   - A library or tool that is released, not deployed
   - Something else / set it up by hand
3. **Where does each part run?** For each part the answer implies, pick the host: Cloudflare, Vercel, Netlify, Render, Fly.io, Railway, or "somewhere Trov does not connect to yet" (the part is still listed; its figures are "—" with that reason).
4. **Connect each host, one at a time.** This is the heart of it. For each host:

ticket.title: Fitted Repo dashboard · 7: a time-boxed experiment, once the groundwork gives it something to aim at
ticket.body:
Part of #145. An experiment with a question and an end date — not a feature.

## Preconditions

Pieces 2 (signals), 3 (the layout description) and 6 (the test set) exist at least in draft. Without them an experiment produces a demo, not an answer.

## The question

Given the signals Trov can have for a repository, how often does a model produce the expected layout, compared with plain rules — and what does it cost per repository?

## Shape

- Run outside the product, against the test set: signals in, a layout in the description out, validated and scored by the rule from piece 6.
- Compare three: rules only; a model only; rules, with a model for what the rules call ambiguous.
- Record accuracy, confident-wrong answers, cost and latency per repository, and what the model was sent.
- Two days, then a write-up with a recommendation: ship rules only, ship the hybrid, or stop.

## Open

- **Which tool or model to prototype with** is the owner's call and is not settled in this issue.
- Nothing from the experiment ships: it informs piece 4's decision.

ticket.title: Fitted Repo dashboard · 6: how we will know it works — a set of real repositories with expected results
ticket.body:
Part of #145. A test set, written before any detector exists.

## Why first

Without agreed answers there is no way to tell a good detector from a confident one, to compare rules with a model, or to notice a regression. This is also what makes an experiment (piece 7) worth running.

## What to collect

- **Ten to fifteen repositories** covering the shapes in the brief: single Worker (`AndresL230/trov`), split frontend and backend (`SaplingLearn/Sapling`), a Next.js app on Vercel, a static site on Netlify, a container service on Fly.io or Render, a monorepo with two deployables, a library published to a registry, a repository with no deploys at all, and two or three deliberately awkward ones (a migration between hosts in progress, two hosts for one part).
- **For each:** the signals Trov would have (from piece 2), the expected shape, the expected layout in the description from piece 3, and what must NOT be shown.
- **The awkward cases' right answer** may be "not sure: ask" — say so explicitly.

## How it is used

- A detector's score is how many repositories get the expected layout, how many get a wrong one stated confidently (the worst outcome), and how many correctly say "not sure".
- Public repositories can be fixtures in the repo; private ones are described, not copied.

## Output

The set as fixtures plus a table, and the scoring rule.

Part of #145. A product design, not code.

- **The three ways in.** (1) Trov proposes a layout and you accept it; (2) you pick from the built-in layouts; (3) you adjust one: reorder, hide, or add a widget. Which of these is in the first version? (Picking a layout needs only piece 3 and may be the whole first release.)

ticket.body:
Part of #145. A design, then the smallest code that proves it.

## Why this is the centre of the whole thing

If a dashboard is a fixed screen, there is nothing for a detector to choose. If it is free-form, nothing can be trusted or tested. The middle is a **fixed catalogue of widgets**, each of which knows how to draw one true thing from data Trov has, and a **description of a layout** that names which widgets appear, in what order, bound to which environment and part.

Today every repository gets the same Repo dashboard, built for one shape of project (a frontend on one host and a backend on another). The idea is for Trov to look at a repository, work out how it is built and hosted, and propose a monitoring screen that fits it — and to let people accept that, pick a different layout, or adjust it.

ticket.title: Repo dashboard: the Cloudflare Worker as the whole stack (Worker, D1, R2 and cron metrics)
ticket.body:
Part of #140.

## Problem

Cloudflare is read today as the FRONTEND host: traffic analytics for a Worker that serves a site, beside a backend whose CPU and memory come from Railway. When the Worker IS the backend too, the figures that matter are different, and the "resources" a service part reports (CPU, memory) do not exist in that form on Workers.

## Wanted

For a part hosted on a Cloudflare Worker that is the whole application:

- **Worker:** requests, error rate, and CPU time (p50 / p99) per range; subrequest or duration limits hit, if the analytics API reports them.
- **D1:** rows read and written per range, and database size.
- **R2:** stored bytes and object count; operations per range if available.
- **Cron triggers:** the last run of each schedule and whether it succeeded.
- **Deploys:** from the Workers Builds check run, as in the one-part issue.

Each figure Cloudflare cannot report through the token an organization gives is "—" with the reason, never `0`.

## Notes

- Polling belongs in the repo cron with a stated request cost per tick, behind the organization's own Cloudflare credential through the existing resolver. State exactly which token permissions are needed (read-only analytics; D1 and R2 read) and show that in Org settings where the credential is entered.
- Confirm each query against a real account before relying on it: the existing Cloudflare and Railway query shapes were written without one and `repo-dashboard.md` says so.
- Decide what replaces the CPU / memory "resources" block for a Worker (CPU time and limits hit are the natural pair).

ticket.title: Repo dashboard: a repository with one environment (drift, previews, the environment list)
ticket.body:
Part of #140.

## Problem

Several things assume at least two long-lived environments:

- **Drift** is computed between environments and "needs two environments"; with one, the section has nothing to say and no way to say why.
- The first configured environment's branch is treated as the head everything else is compared against.
- Branch previews (a build of any branch on its own URL) are neither an environment nor shown anywhere, although for a single-stack project they are the only "staging" there is.

Trov is this case: production from `main`, and a Cloudflare preview per branch.

## Wanted

- With one environment, drift is not an error or an empty box: the section says there is one environment, so there is nothing to compare (the empty-layout pattern in `web/src/skeleton.ts`), and the dashboard's overall status does not depend on it.
- Decide what a preview is: either a lightweight, short-lived entry under the environment ("3 previews, newest 2h ago", each linking to its build) or explicitly out of scope. If shown, they come from captured check runs only, never from a call at render time.
- "What is deployed" for a single environment: the commit production is on, how far `main` is ahead of it (if at all), and when it last deployed.

## Notes

- A preview is not a place to judge health; do not ping preview URLs from the cron.
- Keep the environment budget in the repo cron in mind (`docs/architecture/repo-dashboard.md` › the cron).

ticket.title: Repo dashboard: an environment with one part (no backend / frontend split)
ticket.body:
Part of #140.

## Problem

An environment is modelled as two deployables on two hosts: a backend (a Railway `deployment_status` matched by environment name) and a frontend (the Cloudflare "Workers Builds" `check_run`, matched by name and branch). The environment's status pill, its "last deploy" and its health all read both.

A single-stack project has ONE deployable per environment. For a Worker that serves everything, the only deploy signal is the Workers Builds check run; there is no `deployment_status` at all, and one URL answers for both the app and its API.

## Wanted

- An environment may have exactly one part. Its deploy history, status and "last deploy" come from that one part's signal, whichever kind it is (a check run, or a deployment status).
- Health: one URL (plus an optional health path on the same origin), not a frontend URL and a separate API URL. The pill is computed from the parts that exist.
- The dashboard and Org settings never show a slot for a part that is not configured. No "Backend: not connected" row for a project that has no backend.
- The deploys (CI) section and the MCP `get_repo_dashboard` answer describe the same single part.

## Notes

- The hosting-providers branch already gives a part a `web` / `service` role; a single-stack environment is one part that is both. Decide whether that is a third role or "web with a health path", and say which in `docs/architecture/repo-dashboard.md`.
- Existing two-part configurations (SaplingLearn) must read exactly as they do today.

The Repo dashboard assumes a split deployment. `docs/architecture/repo-dashboard.md` says it outright: "each environment ships two deployables, on two hosts" — a **Backend** read from a Railway `deployment_status`, and a **Frontend** read from the Cloudflare "Workers Builds" `check_run`. ticket.title: Ticket writes over MCP (create, comment, transition, assign, sprint, links)
ticket.body:
## Goal

Let agents work the ticket queue over MCP, not just read it. Today (`feat/tickets`, PR #44) MCP exposes `list_tickets`, `get_ticket`, `list_sprints`, `get_sprint` only; every ticket write is a cookie route under `sessionGate`.

## Proposed tools (bearer, per-person token)

- `create_ticket { title, body?, category?, priority?, assignees?, sprint_id?, link? }` — requester = the bearer's person
- `transition_ticket { id, to }` — same `canTransition` table as the routes; no new statuses
- `comment_ticket { id, body }` — raw text, mentions stay a render concern
- `assign_ticket { id, login, on }`, `set_ticket_sprint { id, sprint_id | null }`, `add_ticket_link { id, raw }`
- `set_ticket_parent { parent_id, child_id }` with the same four rejections

All thin adapters over the existing writers in `src/tools/tickets.ts`, so the transition table, nesting rules, handle validation and `ticket_events` audit rows are shared with the web UI. No new route, no new credential class.

## Decision this needs first

The tickets spec's invariants say "MCP gets read tools only" and "every ticket write is a human authored write". Opening writes over MCP relaxes the first and stretches the second: the write is attributed to the person whose bearer token the agent holds. Options:

1. Attribute to the token's person and record `via: 'mcp'` on `ticket_events` / `ticket_comments` so the UI can mark agent-made changes.
2. Only allow the low-stakes verbs over MCP (create, comment, link) and keep status transitions, assignment and sprint moves human-only.
3. Keep MCP read-only and route agent pr

ticket.title: Handle handoff prompts: store a session's handoff and route it to whoever picks the work up
ticket.body:
**Canopy feature addition.**

## What
An agent or a person often ends a working session with a **handoff prompt**: a self-contained brief that the next session pastes in to pick up the work. The next session might be the same person later, a teammate, or another agent. The brief covers what was done, what's left, where the state lives, and what not to redo. Today these live in terminal scrollback, chat or one-off files, so they get lost or go stale.

Canopy should treat handoff prompts as first-class records:
- **Write.** An MCP tool, and/or an option on `record-session`, stores a handoff with:
  - the author;
  - an optional recipient (a handle, or open to anyone);
  - the repo or area;
  - links to issues, PRs, tickets and sprints.
- **Read.**
  - The recipient sees pending handoffs in My Work.
  - `load-context` surfaces handoffs relevant to the area being worked.
  - A tool fetches one by id, so an agent can start from it directly.
- **Lifecycle.** A handoff goes open → picked up (by whom, when) → done or superseded, so it isn't run twice or after it has gone stale.

## Open questions
- **Direct or staged?** A handoff is somebody's request, so it probably follows the ticket model (direct write, scoped) rather than the staging gate. Or should a handoff simply be a ticket with a `handoff` kind?
- **Freshness.** Should a handoff record the commit or branch it was written against, so a reader can tell when it is out of date?
- **Secrets.** Handoffs often paste environment details and URLs. Should they be scrubbed the way feed entries are?

ticket.title: Store and share artifacts: keep agent-produced pages (specs, reports, design pages) in Canopy and share them with the team
ticket.body:
**Canopy feature addition.**

## What
Agent sessions increasingly produce shareable **artifacts**: design pages, specs, audit reports, dashboards. One example is the Google sign-in design page linked from `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-14-google-signin-identity-design.md`. Today they live at scattered URLs or in local files, and are hard to find later.

Canopy should store them and share them with the team:
- **Store.** Register an artifact through MCP and the web. A record holds:
  - a title and kind;
  - a URL or an uploaded file;
  - the author and the repo or area;
  - links to issues, PRs, tickets and sprints.
- **Share.** Browse artifacts by area, sprint or ticket. They are visible to the org, and can be attached to tickets and sprints as resources.
- **Search.** Include artifacts in `query`, so `load-context` can surface them.

This is not the existing feed-entry `artifacts` field, which holds observed PR, commit and issue references on a feed row. The naming should avoid colliding with it.

## Open questions
- **Store the content, or only a link?** Links rot, and a private artifact page isn't viewable by teammates. Copies (e.g. in R2) need a size limit and access control.
- **Direct or staged?** An authored artifact is closer to a ticket than to a doc. But one presented as a spec or decision may need to go through the gate before it counts as authoritative.
- **Access.** Org-wide by default, or private to the author with explicit sharing?

ticket.title: Feed: typed entries with a type-driven layout (a small generative UI for the Feed)
ticket.body:
## Idea
A feed entry now has one of six **types**, each with a fixed set of labelled lines — but only by convention, in the `record-session` skill (#62):

| Type | Lines |
|---|---|
| `Shipped:` | What · Why · Impact · Follow-up |
| `Decision:` | Decided · Because · Instead of |
| `Triage:` | Closed · Kept · Moved to · Why |
| `Status:` | State · Blocked on · Next |
| `Finding:` | Found · Evidence · So |
| `Incident:` | What broke · Cause · Fix · Guard |

Today the Feed renders every entry the same way: a headline and a markdown body. **Make the type drive how the entry looks** — a small generative UI: the agent supplies typed, structured content; the Feed picks the layout.

## What it could look like
- A **type chip** on the card (tone per type: Incident red, Status amber, Shipped accent, …) and a **type filter** in the Feed header next to the author filter.
- A **layout per type** rather than one markdown blob, e.g.
  - *Shipped* — What as the lead line, Why/Impact as quiet secondary lines, PR chips prominent;
  - *Triage* — Closed / Kept / Moved to as three compact columns of issue/PR chips;
  - *Status* — a "Blocked on" list with an owner-only marker, Next as a footer;
  - *Finding* — the measured result pulled out as a figure (`2/6 → 5/6`);
  - *Incident* — a mini timeline: broke → cause → fix → guard.
- Entries without a type (everything written before this) keep today's layout.

ticket.title: MCP assign_ticket: let agents (un)assign existing tickets
ticket.body:
## Why
Agents can file tickets with assignees (`create_ticket`), but once a ticket exists nothing an agent does can change who owns it:
- There's no MCP assign tool. #45 proposed `assign_ticket` and deliberately kept assignment human-only.
- GitHub assignment doesn't reach mirrored tickets. `src/tools/ticket-mirror.ts` seeds assignees at import only ("a GitHub (un)assign never touches assignees").

That surfaced on 2026-09-27, when an agent split the Sapling beta work across the team. It could assign on GitHub, but about 16 existing tickets had to be assigned by hand in the web UI. Teammates who don't use GitHub (the incoming UI/UX designers) can't be reached through GitHub at all.

## Proposal
Add the MCP tool #45 sketched, as a thin adapter over the writer the web UI already uses:

`assign_ticket { id, login, on: boolean }`: add (`on: true`) or remove (`on: false`) one assignee.
- It reuses the web UI's handle validation, so an unknown handle is `bad_request`.
- It's attributed to the bearer and writes a `ticket_events` row (or the existing assignment audit, if assignment has its own), marked `via: 'mcp'` if that marker exists by then.
- It's idempotent: adding someone already assigned, or removing someone who isn't, is a no-op success.
- It never changes status. Assigning doesn't auto-move `submitted → in_progress` unless the web UI already does that, in which case it matches the UI exactly.

ticket.title: Let people create their own organization (self-serve org creation)

Self-serve organization creation is switched off for now. Only a platform superadmin adds an organization (Platform › Add organization) and names its admin.

## Current state (PR #93)

ticket.title: Connect repositories through a GitHub App instead of a pasted token and a hand-made webhook
ticket.body:
Today an organization's admin connects GitHub by hand: they create a fine-grained personal access token with the right permissions, paste it into Org settings › Integrations, then add a webhook in the repository's GitHub settings with a URL and a generated secret. That is fine for orgs onboarded by hand, and it is where setup will fail for orgs we don't know. A GitHub App would make Trov something an admin installs on their repositories.

## What it replaces

| | Today | With a GitHub App |
|---|---|---|
| Connecting a repo | Create a token with seven read permissions, paste it in | Click Install, pick the repos |
| Live events | Add a webhook by hand per repo (`/webhook/github/:hookId` + secret) | One App webhook, delivered automatically |
| Credential | Long-lived, tied to one person; breaks when they leave or it expires | Short-lived installation tokens minted by Trov |
| Org-owned repos | The GitHub org may have to approve fine-grained tokens | An org owner approves the install once |
| Several repos | One webhook each; only the primary repo's events are captured | Every selected repo delivers through the App |
| Which repos exist | The admin types `owner/repo` | Trov lists what the installation can see |

It works the same for personal repos (`username/project`) and org repos (`orgname/project`).

## What it does not change

- Cloudflare analytics, Railway and the app-metrics endpoint stay as pasted credentials.
- Invitations, memberships and roles stay Trov's own data.

ticket.title: Hosting providers: a provider interface so the Repo dashboard is not tied to Cloudflare and Railway
ticket.body:
The Repo dashboard's usage and deploy panels are built around one stack: a Cloudflare Worker frontend (requests and error rate from Cloudflare's analytics API) and a Railway backend (CPU and memory from Railway's API). An org on any other host gets the GitHub half and health pings only; the other panels say "Not connected".

This is the umbrella issue for making that pluggable. Per-provider issues link here.

## Today

- Integration kinds are a fixed list in the schema and code: `cloudflare_analytics`, `railway`, `metrics_endpoint`, `github_token`, `github_webhook` (`org_secrets.kind` CHECK, `src/integrations/catalog.ts`, `src/data/secrets.ts`).
- An environment row has Cloudflare- and Railway-specific columns (`worker`, `worker_check`, `railway_env`, `railway_environment_id`, `railway_service_id`).
- The pollers are per provider (`pollCloudflare`, `pollRailway` in `src/repo/poll.ts`) and the dashboard projection names them (`cf_*`, `rw_*` metrics).
- Already provider-neutral: health pings (any https URL), GitHub deployments / check runs / workflow runs, and the app-metrics endpoint an org implements itself.

## Proposed shape

- A **provider** describes: its id and label, the credential(s) it needs and where an admin gets them, per-environment settings (project / service / site ids), a `probe` (Test connection), and one or more `poll` functions that return normalised series.
- **Normalised metrics**, so the dashboard does not care who produced them: requests, error rate, latency for a "web" part; CPU, memory for a "service" part; deploys with status and commit.

ticket.title: Hosting provider: Vercel
ticket.body:
Add **Vercel** as a hosting provider behind the provider interface (#97).

## Scope

Projects and deployments from the Vercel REST API with a team-scoped access token; usage where the plan exposes it (requests, errors, function duration). Deploy status also arrives through GitHub deployments. Per-environment setting: project id and team id; map Trov environments to Vercel's production / preview targets.

## Done when

- An org admin can pick Vercel for an environment's part, enter its credential and ids in Org settings, and Test connection passes against the real API.
- The Repo dashboard shows that environment's deploys and whatever usage Vercel exposes, in the same panels Cloudflare and Railway fill today.
- The credential goes to Vercel's API host only, errors are scrubbed, and an org without it costs no requests.
- The Set form says where to get the credential and the narrowest permission that works; verify that against the live API, not from memory.

Depends on #97.

ticket.title: Hosting provider: AWS (later)
ticket.body:
Track **AWS** as a hosting provider behind the provider interface (#97). Not needed yet; the consumer hosts come first.

## Why it is its own piece

- There is no single API: an app may be on ECS, Lambda, App Runner, Amplify, Elastic Beanstalk or plain EC2, with metrics in CloudWatch.
- Credentials should be a cross-account IAM role an org grants Trov (assume-role with an external id), not long-lived access keys, which needs SigV4 signing in the Worker.
- Scope must be read-only and narrow (CloudWatch metrics for named resources, deployment status), per org.

## First cut, when picked up

- CloudWatch metrics for one named service (requests / errors from an ALB or API Gateway; CPU / memory from ECS or Lambda) through an assumed role.
- Deploy status from GitHub deployments, as today.

Depends on #97.
